explanation: Stonehenge in Wiltshire is a World Heritage Site, probably a place of religious and ceremonial importance built in the Bronze Age.

angles.q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
Stonehenge is an example of what?

explanation: The first farmers arrived in Britain about 6,000 years ago, probably from south-east Europe, and built houses, tombs and monuments.

angles.q: Roughly how long ago did the first farmers arrive in Britain?
What did the first farmers in Britain build to bury their dead?

explanation: In the Bronze Age, about 4,000 years ago, people learned to make bronze from copper and tin. They lived in roundhouses.

angles.q: Bronze is made by combining copper with which other metal?
Roughly how long ago did the Bronze Age begin in Britain?

explanation: Maiden Castle in Dorset is one of the most impressive Iron Age hill forts that survives in Britain.

angles.q: In which county is the Iron Age hill fort of Maiden Castle?

explanation: The Romans built roads and public buildings, created a structure of law, and introduced new plants and animals to Britain.

angles.q: Which of these did the Romans introduce to Britain?
Roman roads in Britain were mainly built for what purpose?

explanation: By about AD 600, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were established in Britain, mainly in what is now England. The west of Britain remained largely Celtic.

angles.q: Which part of Britain remained largely free of Anglo-Saxon rule?
The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were established mainly in which part of Britain?

explanation: Sutton Hoo in Suffolk is the burial place of an Anglo-Saxon king, buried in a ship surrounded by treasure and armour.

angles.q: In which county is the Anglo-Saxon burial site of Sutton Hoo?
An Anglo-Saxon king at Sutton Hoo was buried inside what?

explanation: The Vikings first came to Britain in AD 789 to raid coastal towns and take goods and slaves, and later began to settle.

angles.q: What did the Vikings do when they first came to Britain?

explanation: The Normans built castles across England and Wales to control the land they had conquered.

angles.q: Why did the Normans build castles across England and Wales?
angles.a: To control the land they had conquered
wrong: To store grain for the winter

explanation: The Norman Conquest of 1066 was the last successful foreign invasion of England.

angles.q: The Norman Conquest was the last successful what?

explanation: The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 annexed Wales to the Crown of England, following Edward I's campaign against the Welsh.

angles.q: In which year was the Statute of Rhuddlan?
Which English king annexed Wales through the Statute of Rhuddlan?

explanation: Edward I built a ring of castles in Wales, including Conwy and Caernarfon, to hold the country after his conquest.

angles.q: Caernarfon and Conwy are examples of what, built by Edward I?

explanation: The Hundred Years War between England and France lasted from 1337 to 1453, a total of 116 years.

angles.q: In which year did the Hundred Years War begin?
The Hundred Years War was fought between England and which country?

explanation: The Wars of the Roses began in 1455 and were fought between the House of Lancaster and the House of York.

angles.q: In which year did the Wars of the Roses begin?
Which house was represented by a red rose?

explanation: William Caxton was the first person in England to print books using a printing press.

angles.q: What did William Caxton introduce to England?

explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales, a series of poems in English about a group of pilgrims travelling to Canterbury.

angles.q: The pilgrims in The Canterbury Tales were travelling to which city?
In which language did Geoffrey Chaucer write The Canterbury Tales?

explanation: Wales was formally united with England during the reign of Henry VIII, and the Welsh sent representatives to the English Parliament.

angles.q: After Wales was united with England, where did Welsh representatives sit?

explanation: Mary I was a devout Catholic who persecuted Protestants, earning the nickname Bloody Mary. She was succeeded by Elizabeth I.

angles.q: Which monarch was known as Bloody Mary?
Who succeeded Mary I on the throne of England?

explanation: Elizabeth I was a Protestant who reached a compromise between Catholics and Protestants that became the basis of the Church of England.

angles.q: What was Elizabeth I's religion?

explanation: William Shakespeare lived and wrote during the Tudor and early Stuart periods, and his plays were performed at the Globe Theatre.

angles.q: In which London theatre were many of Shakespeare's plays performed?

explanation: The King James Version of the Bible, also called the Authorised Version, was produced during the reign of James I.

angles.q: The King James Bible is also known by what name?

explanation: During the English Civil War, supporters of the king were called Cavaliers and supporters of Parliament were called Roundheads.

angles.q: Supporters of the king during the Civil War were known as what?

explanation: Oliver Cromwell died in 1658 and was briefly succeeded as Lord Protector by his son Richard, before the monarchy was restored in 1660.

angles.q: Who briefly succeeded Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector?

explanation: The Royal Society was formed in about 1660 to promote natural knowledge and is the oldest surviving scientific society in the world.

angles.q: The Royal Society was formed to promote what?

explanation: William III defeated James II at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland in 1690, an event still commemorated by some in Northern Ireland.

angles.q: In which year was the Battle of the Boyne?
In which country was the Battle of the Boyne fought?

explanation: After 1688 the monarch could no longer raise taxes or keep an army without the agreement of Parliament, and Britain became a constitutional monarchy.

angles.q: After 1688, what could the monarch no longer do without Parliament's agreement?
angles.a: Raise taxes or keep an army

explanation: During the Highland Clearances, many Scottish landlords destroyed small farms to make way for sheep, and many people emigrated.

angles.q: During the Highland Clearances, small farms were cleared to make way for what?
Many people affected by the Highland Clearances did what?

explanation: By 1913 the British Empire covered about a quarter of the world's population and was the largest empire the world has seen.

angles.q: By which year did the British Empire cover about a quarter of the world's population?

explanation: William Wilberforce, an evangelical Christian and MP, led the parliamentary campaign to abolish the slave trade.

angles.q: William Wilberforce campaigned against what?

explanation: Florence Nightingale served in the Crimean War and later established a nursing school. She is considered the founder of modern nursing.

angles.q: In which war did Florence Nightingale serve?
Where did Florence Nightingale set up her nursing school?

explanation: The Reform Act of 1832 abolished many rotten boroughs and greatly increased the number of people who could vote.

angles.q: In which year was the Reform Act that greatly increased the number of voters?
What did the Reform Act of 1832 abolish?

explanation: Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western Railway, bridges and steamships including the SS Great Britain.

angles.q: Which railway did Isambard Kingdom Brunel build?

explanation: George Stephenson built early steam locomotives, and Britain led the world in developing the railway.

angles.q: George Stephenson is associated with the development of what?

explanation: The British suffered around 60,000 casualties on the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916.

angles.q: In which war was the Battle of the Somme fought?

explanation: The Blitz was the sustained bombing of London and other British cities by the German air force during the Second World War.

angles.q: During which war did the Blitz take place?

explanation: Alan Turing helped break German codes at Bletchley Park during the Second World War and is regarded as a founder of computer science.

angles.q: At which site did Alan Turing work on breaking German codes?
Alan Turing is regarded as a founder of which field?

explanation: Sir Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 and shared the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1945.

angles.q: In which year did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin?
What did Alexander Fleming discover?

explanation: John Logie Baird, a Scottish inventor, made the first television broadcast of a moving picture in 1924.

angles.q: Which invention is John Logie Baird credited with demonstrating?

explanation: Sir Frank Whittle, a British RAF engineer, developed the jet engine in the 1930s.

angles.q: Which invention is Sir Frank Whittle credited with?

explanation: Sir Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe pioneered IVF, and the world's first test-tube baby was born in Britain in 1978.

angles.q: In which country was the world's first test-tube baby born?

explanation: Dolly the sheep was cloned at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh in 1996, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

angles.q: Near which city was Dolly the sheep cloned?
What kind of animal was Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell?

explanation: The NHS was established in 1948 by the Labour government led by Clement Attlee, with Aneurin Bevan as Minister for Health.

angles.q: Which Prime Minister led the government that founded the NHS?

explanation: Margaret Thatcher became the UK's first female Prime Minister in 1979 and was the longest-serving Prime Minister of the 20th century.

angles.q: Who was the UK's first female Prime Minister?

explanation: After the Second World War, many countries of the British Empire gained independence, and most joined the Commonwealth.

angles.q: Most former British colonies that became independent joined what?

explanation: After the Second World War the UK needed workers to rebuild, and encouraged migration from the West Indies, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

angles.q: Why did the UK encourage migration after the Second World War?
angles.a: There was a shortage of workers to rebuild the country
wrong: To increase the size of the army
To replace people who had emigrated
